title: Why Public Education Is Failing And How You Can Fix It
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Sparked by an email he saw assigning a struggling group of students an 'easier' alternative project because they failed benchmarks 'through no fault of their own,' Linsin argues that American schools have made a systemic habit of stripping responsibility from students and calling it compassion. He lists the ways students are routinely shielded from failure and excuse-making, and contends that lightening the burden of responsibility on students actually makes them perform worse across listening, learning, and behavior, while denying them the pride and self-belief that comes from real accountability. He is careful to note that genuine learning disabilities are real and deserve accommodation, but argues that too many students are funneled into that category as an excuse. The piece ends by framing this as a two-way responsibility contract: students must own their work, and teachers must own holding them to real standards rather than papering over failure with fake grades and 'do-nothing credit.'
points: When students fail to meet requirements, ask directly 'whose fault was it' rather than accepting the framing that it was 'no fault of their own.'
Students denied real responsibility from an early age are, in Linsin's view, never actually expected to do their own work and have their grades inflated to mask it.
The students who most need real responsibility (from poverty, broken homes, gang violence) are often given the least of it.
Real, unavoidable responsibility gives students pride, self-worth, and proof they can overcome obstacles — letting them off the hook only feels good in the moment.
Teachers' half of the responsibility contract is to hold students accountable and demand independently completed work, not just to expect students to behave.
quotes: Evidently, this group of students failed to meet a series of benchmarks leading up to the due date, which was in mere days.

If the students’ failed—and let’s be honest, they did—then who dropped the ball? And how were the rest of students able to fulfill the requirements over the weeks and months leading up to the final project?

There is so much fear of looking bad (or worse than we already do) that we would rather sacrifice our students and their future by ignoring their pitiful academic skills and passing them along until they’re out of the system and no more our problem.

Yet tens of thousands of teachers and administrators, brainwashed by the idea that high standards of behavior and demanding applied study are mean and/or discriminatory, will deny this is happening to your face while continuing to do it every single day.
The larger point is that when we lighten the weight of responsibility to listen, learn, and behave students do much worse in all three.
Sadly, the very students who need it the most—from broken homes, poverty, and gang violence—are given the least amount of responsibility.

While students must take responsibility for their job—which is to listen, learn, and behave—we as teachers must take responsibility for ours—which is to hold them accountable for behavior that is required for success in school.
